plain_english: Before you start anything, think about what comes before and what comes after. Then decide if you want to do it. Otherwise you'll start with excitement, ignore the consequences, and when reality hits, you'll quit in shame. "I want to win at the Olympics." Fine. But think about what that really means. If it's worth it, then go for it. You'll have to follow strict rules. You'll have to diet and give up treats. You'll have to train your body at set times, whether you feel like it or not, in heat and cold. No cold water. Sometimes no wine. You'll have to surrender completely to your trainer like a patient to a doctor. Then in the actual competition, you might get thrown in a ditch, dislocate your arm, twist your ankle, swallow a mouthful of dust, get beaten up, and still lose. Once you've counted up all of this, if you still want it, then start training.
original_excerpt: In every affair consider what precedes and what follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit, indeed, careless of the consequences, and when these are developed, you will shamefully desist. "I would conquer at the Olympic Games." But consider what precedes and what follows, and then, if it be for your advantage, engage in the affair. You must conform to rules, submit to a diet, refrain from dainties; exercise your body, whether you choose it or not, at a stated hour, in heat and cold; you must drink no cold water, and sometimes no wine—in a word, you must give yourself up to your trainer as to a physician. Then, in the combat, you may be thrown into a ditch, dislocate your arm, turn your ankle, swallow an abundance of dust, receive stripes [for negligence], and, after all, lose the victory. When you have reckoned up all this, if your inclination still holds, set about the combat.

plain_english: Without proper planning, you'll act like children playing games. Kids pretend to be wrestlers, then gladiators, then trumpet players, then actors — copying whatever show impressed them last. You'll do the same thing. One day you'll be a wrestler, the next a gladiator. Now a philosopher, now a public speaker. But you won't take any of it seriously. Like a monkey, you'll copy everything you see. Each new thing will excite you until it becomes boring. Why? Because you never think things through. You never study the whole situation and test it properly. You just jump in carelessly with half-hearted effort.
original_excerpt: Otherwise, take notice, you will behave like children who sometimes play wrestlers, sometimes gladiators, sometimes blow a trumpet, and sometimes act a tragedy, when they happen to have seen and admired these shows. Thus you too will be at one time a wrestler, and another a gladiator; now a philosopher, now an orator; but nothing in earnest. Like an ape you mimic all you see, and one thing after another is sure to please you, but is out of favor as soon as it becomes familiar. For you have never entered upon anything considerately; nor after having surveyed and tested the whole matter, but carelessly, and with a halfway zeal.

plain_english: Some people hear a philosopher speak — someone like Euphrates, though really, who can speak like him? — and suddenly they want to be philosophers too. But first, think about what this actually means. Consider what you're capable of. If you wanted to be a wrestler, you'd check your shoulders, your back, your thighs. Different people are built for different things. Do you think you can keep living exactly as you do now and be a philosopher? Can you keep eating, drinking, getting angry, and complaining like you always have? You'll have to stay alert. You'll have to work hard. You'll have to control certain desires. You'll have to leave your friends behind. Your servants will look down on you. People will laugh at you. You'll lose out to others in everything — jobs, honors, court cases.
original_excerpt: Thus some, when they have seen a philosopher and heard a man speaking like Euphrates[3]—though, indeed, who can speak like him?—have a mind to be philosophers, too. Consider first, man, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear. If you would be a wrestler, consider your shoulders, your back, your thighs; for different persons are made for different things. Do you think that you can act as you do and be a philosopher, that you can eat, drink, be angry, be discontented, as you are now? You must watch, you must labor, you must get the better of certain appetites, must quit your acquaintances, be despised by your servant, be laughed at by those you meet; come off worse than others in everything—in offices, in honors, before tribunals.

plain_english: Think about all this carefully. Then decide. If you're willing to give up those things to gain peace, freedom, and calm — go ahead and start. If not, don't bother. Don't be like children who play at being different things — first a philosopher, then a tax collector, then a speaker, then one of Caesar's officials. These roles don't mix. You must be one person, either good or bad. You must develop either your own thinking or chase external things. Focus either on what's within you or what's outside you. Be either a philosopher or just another person in the crowd.
original_excerpt: When you have fully considered all these things, approach, if you please—that is, if, by parting with them, you have a mind to purchase serenity, freedom, and tranquillity. If not, do not come hither; do not, like children, be now a philosopher, then a publican, then an orator, and then one of Caesar's officers. These things are not consistent. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
